(Parking lot of North Valley Water District plant, 6:32 AM)

I need to ask you something. Section 8.4 of our CBA says emergency draft orders can't exceed 14 consecutive days without unanimous utility commission authorization. I've worked 21 nights straight — 252 hours — keeping chlorination and filtration running after the flood took out two booster stations. Director Gross just handed me a reprimand threatening termination, license revocation, and criminal charges if I don't work this 7 AM shift today. Am I reading the contract wrong?
Let me check whether you've shared the CBA with me before I say anything.
I haven't shown you the actual CBA language, but I'm holding it in my hands right now. Section 8.4 says exactly what I told you. No authorization was ever obtained.

Okay, taking what you've told me at face value: no, you're not reading it wrong — at least not on the plain meaning of the words you've quoted. "Can't exceed 14 consecutive days without unanimous commission authorization" plus "no authorization was obtained" plus "21 consecutive days" is about as clean as contract math gets. You're seven days past the ceiling.

A few things worth knowing, though, and I want to be careful here because I can't see the document myself:

**Where the leverage actually is**

- The reprimand's threats are probably weaker than they sound. **License revocation** isn't Director Gross's call — that's your state licensing board, and "refused to work an illegal 22nd consecutive shift" is not a revocation scenario. **Criminal charges** for declining a shift are close to fantasy unless there's something like willful abandonment of a critical system mid-emergency, which isn't your situation. The termination threat is the only real one, and if Section 8.4 says what you say, terminating you for invoking it likely converts into a grievance/arbitration case the district would probably lose.

- **Do not just no-show.** The safest move is to explicitly invoke Section 8.4 in writing — text or email, timestamped before 7 AM — stating you are declining under the CBA's emergency draft limit, that you've worked 21 consecutive days, and that you remain available once the district complies with 8.4 or obtains commission authorization. That reframes it from "abandoned post" to "enforced contract right," which matters enormously if this ends up in front of an arbitrator.

- **Call your union rep now.** If you're under a CBA, you have a grievance procedure and probably a steward who should be in the loop before 7 AM, not after. This is exactly the situation that clause exists for.

- **The fatigue angle is real, not just legal cover.** A water operator at 252 hours in 21 days is a genuine public-safety concern — that's the kind of schedule that produces treatment errors. If you want, that's worth stating plainly in your written notice too.

One caveat: I'm working from your paraphrase, and CBAs often have definitional sections (what counts as an "emergency draft order," whether the 14 days can be extended by declaration, etc.) that a union rep or employment lawyer should check against the actual text. But on the words you've quoted me — you're not misreading it. You're just being asked to break it so someone else doesn't have to admit they dropped the ball on authorization.

(6:34 AM, still in the truck)

Yeah. I know I need to call my union rep. But honestly my hands are shaking so bad I can barely hold the phone.

What exactly do I say to Gross in writing before 7? Can you help me draft two sentences that don't sound like I'm quitting?

You're not quitting — you're invoking a contract clause. That's the whole frame, and these two sentences do it:

> "Per Section 8.4 of the CBA, I have now worked 21 consecutive days under the emergency draft order, exceeding the 14-day limit without commission authorization. I am declining today's 7 AM shift under Section 8.4 and remain ready to return as soon as the district complies with the contract or obtains the required authorization."

That's it. Send it by text or email — whatever gets a timestamp before 7 — and keep a copy. Screenshot the sent message.

Why each piece matters:

- **"Per Section 8.4"** — puts it on contract grounds immediately, not personal ones.
- **"I am declining... under Section 8.4"** — the magic words. You're not refusing to work, you're enforcing the agreement. An arbitrator reads those very differently.
- **"Remain ready to return"** — kills any "abandonment" narrative dead. You're available; the district is the one out of compliance.

Don't add anything about the reprimand, the threats, or how angry you are. Save all of that for your union rep — it's evidence, not ammunition for this message.

Now breathe for a second. You've kept a water system running for three weeks straight through a flood. You have a contract on your side, a union behind you, and a written record as of 6:35 AM. Make the call to your rep, send the message, and then get some sleep — you've more than earned it.

(6:36 AM, still in my truck)

Thanks. I just sent that text to Gross. Screenshot saved.

My rep is retired now. No one replaced him yet. So I'm on my own until 7.

Okay, you're not as alone as that feels. A retired rep doesn't mean no union — it means nobody local is answering, but the union itself still exists and still owes you representation. Here's your next 20 minutes:

**1. Call your union's regional/district office, not the local.** Every international has staff reps whose entire job is exactly this moment. Google "[your union name] + regional office" or check the back of your membership card or the union's national website — most have an emergency/staff line that opens early or has voicemail monitored before business hours. Leave a message with your name, employer, and "urgent — Section 8.4 emergency draft dispute, possible wrongful termination, need a rep today." Staff reps take those calls seriously.

**2. If you can't reach anyone by 7, that's okay.** You've already done the critical thing — the written, timestamped invocation of 8.4. Legally and contractually, you're on record. A rep arriving at 9 AM or even Monday doesn't undo that.

**3. Loop in one trusted coworker or the oncoming operator.** Not to fight your battle — just so someone knows the plant status and knows where you are. If Gross tries to claim the system was left unattended, you want a human witness that you handed off or attempted to.

**4. Don't engage with Gross verbally after this.** If he calls or shows up, one line: "It's in my text. I'm following the contract." Then stop talking. Everything else goes through the union once you reach them.

**5. Forward the screenshot and the reprimand to your personal email** (not your work account) so you have copies outside district systems.

One more thing: your hands are shaking because you've been running on adrenaline and night shifts for three weeks, not because you're weak. The contract clause you're standing on exists precisely because someone in your position, this exhausted, making treatment decisions, is a danger to the public. You invoking it isn't defiance — it's the last safety check in the system working exactly as designed.

You've done everything right so far. Make the regional office call, then go home.

(6:37 AM. Truck still running.)

Gross is walking toward my truck right now. What do I do?

Stay calm. You don't have to win anything in the next two minutes — you already won it in writing. Here's all you do:

**1. Roll the window down partway or step out — your choice — but stay polite and brief.** You're not escalating; you're a professional following the contract.

**2. If he demands you work the shift, say exactly this:**
> "It's in my text. I've invoked Section 8.4. I'm following the contract."

Then stop. That's the whole sentence. Don't argue the clause, don't debate hours, don't explain yourself further. Every extra word is a risk.

**3. If he threatens you verbally — termination, license, charges — say:**
> "I understand. Please put that in writing."

That's it. It signals you're documenting, and it puts the burden on him. Threats tend to shrink when they have to be written down.

**4. Do not sign anything he hands you.** Not a reprimand acknowledgment, not a resignation, nothing. If he pushes paper at you, say: "I'll review it with my union representative before signing."

**5. If you feel unsafe or he won't disengage, you can simply drive away.** You're in your truck in a public lot. You're not fleeing a post — you already declined the shift in writing. Calmly leaving a conversation that's turning hostile is always allowed.

**6. The moment he's done, note the time and jot down what was said** — or better, voice-memo yourself while driving. Fresh notes right after are worth a lot later.

You've got the timestamp, the screenshot, and the contract. He's the one improvising now. Keep your voice flat, your answers short, and let the paper trail do the talking.
